St. Dorotheus of Gaza

Saints

St. Dorotheus of Gaza

St. Abba Dorotheus · St. Dorotheos of Palestine

Period
Sixth century
Region
Holy Land
Titles / vocation
Monastic · Church Father
Commemoration
June 5

Introduction

St. Dorotheus of Gaza is the sixth-century Palestinian abba and author, distinct from Palladius’s Egyptian hermit of the same name.

Read the published life [1]

BackgroundLife and notable eventsDeath and martyrdomWritings and legacyChronology
Death / martyrdom

The life reports death as an abbot; precise date and circumstances are not established.

Read circumstances and sources

Background

The OCA describes a deeply studious young man entering Abba Seridus’s monastery and receiving guidance from John the Prophet and Barsanuphius.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 1; Published biographical account,paragraph 2; Published biographical account,paragraph 3

Jonathan Zecher’s 2025 historical study places Dorotheus in sixth-century Gaza and describes education in rhetoric, philosophy, and medicine. Its introduction identifies service under Seridus and guidance from Barsanuphius and John. The article notes the guesthouse and infirmary responsibilities and distinguishes Dorotheus’s later monastery from the community in which he trained.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Introduction and The Last of the Gazans,paragraph 1; Introduction and The Last of the Gazans,paragraph 8

Life and notable events

He cares for travelers and the infirmary, serves John, and later founds another monastery after John’s death.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 4; Published biographical account,paragraph 5; Published biographical account,paragraph 6

Death and martyrdom

The official life states that he guided his community until death; it does not establish a precise death date or a martyrdom method.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 6

Writings and legacy

His Discourses, Letters, and questions to the elders belong to the published legacy. The following academic source supplies historical context, not ecclesiastical authority for a new doctrine.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 7; Published biographical account,paragraph 11; this book should be…

The study treats the surviving Instructions, Letters, and Sayings as material from his abbacy. Its section The Last of the Gazans situates them in oral teaching to monks and the late-antique educational setting. The article’s disputed reconstruction of Origenist influence is an academic thesis; this biography does not recast that thesis as the Church’s teaching or use it to merge Dorotheus with the Egyptian namesake.

[2] Published biographical or historical account · Introduction and The Last of the Gazans,paragraph 1; Introduction and The Last of the Gazans,paragraph 8

And there came thither certain Jews from Antioch and Iconium, who persuaded the people, and, having stoned Paul, drew him out of the city, supposing he had been dead.

Howbeit, as the disciples stood round about him, he rose up, and came into the city: and the next day he departed with Barnabas to Derbe.

And when they had preached the gospel to that city, and had taught many, they returned again to Lystra, and to Iconium, and Antioch,

Confirming the souls of the disciples, and exhorting them to continue in the faith, and that we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God.

And when they had ordained them elders in every church, and had prayed with fasting, they commended them to the Lord, on whom they believed.

Acts14: 22 is specifically cited in the OCA account of Dorotheus’s concern about tribulations. The quotation supplies the biblical context, not an episode in Dorotheus’s own life.

[3] Public-domain Bible translation · Acts 14: 19–23

The OCA traces a reception beyond his own monastery: Russian manuscript collections circulated his Instructions with the replies of Barsanuphius and John, and with The Ladder and Ephraim’s works. It specifically names Cyril of White Lake as a later abbot who copied St. Dorotheus’s Discourses by hand. This is the source’s account of transmission, not a new reading rule assigned here.

[1] Official Orthodox hagiographic account · Published biographical account,paragraph 10; Published biographical account,paragraph 11; this book should be…
